title: LTA directs Grab to pause some AV testing after near miss with schoolgirl in Punggol
Monster shares fall as weaker margins highlight cost burden
article:
(Nov 7): Monster Beverage Corp shares fell as much as 8.2% on Friday, the biggest decline in over two years, after the energy drink giant’s weaker-than-expected margins underscored the impact of soaring costs in the beverage industry.

Third-quarter (3Q) gross profit margin was 54.7%, down from 55.7% a year ago and short of the 55.4% analysts had estimated.

Monster and other beverage companies have been grappling with higher costs due to the impact of US tariffs and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which have driven up the price of the aluminium used for their cans. Monster expects continued increases in aluminium costs through at least the first quarter of 2027, executives said on a call with analysts on Thursday.

Smaller rival Celsius Holdings Inc also warned that stubbornly high commodity costs are weighing on its margins.

Monster’s 3Q sales rose more than expected, as the energy drink giant continues to see booming demand for its beverages outside of the US. But pricing for Monster’s drinks in international markets tends to be substantially lower than in the US, adding further pressure on profitability.

See also: US tech stocks rebound as investors weigh valuations after rout

The company saw continued strength abroad, driven by Brazil, with sales in the international segment jumping 28% to represent nearly half of Monster’s overall sales in the period. Total net sales rose 17% to US$2.56 billion, ahead of the US$2.49 billion analysts were expecting.

While the commodity costs “aren’t helping,” a US price increase planned for November should help offset some of the compression, Jefferies analysts led by Kaumil Gajrawala wrote in a post-earnings note. “The top line matters more, and it’s intact,” they added.

As demand for beverages that aren’t typical sodas or coffees explodes, Monster has been trying to get its products in front of new costumers that are trying energy drinks for the first time. It’s expanding its social media presence, highlighting both longtime offerings and new launches, including a forthcoming protein energy drink.

See also: Nasdaq 100 sinks 6% as chipmaker selloff deepens

It’s also seeing growth in multipacks as consumers look for value, but isn’t being hit as hard by the consumer pullback that’s hammered restaurants and fast food. “Energy drinks always have been regarded as an affordable luxury,” Chief executive officer Hilton Schlosberg said on the call.

US consumer sentiment unexpectedly rises, fuelled by independents
article:
(Nov 6): US consumer sentiment rose in November to a three-month high, bolstered by modest improvements in Americans' views of their personal finances and the economic outlook.

The University of Michigan’s preliminary sentiment index increased to 51 in November from 48 in October, according to the survey released Friday. The median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists projected sentiment to hold at 48.

The improvement was concentrated among independents, who reported the strongest consumer sentiment in more than a year. Sentiment across both Democrats and Republicans deteriorated.

Cost of living concerns remain top of mind for many Americans. About 57% of respondents spontaneously mentioned that high prices had eroded their living standards — the highest since May.

Despite limited lay-offs and strong economic growth, household finances have been squeezed as prices rise faster than wages. Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterm elections reflected deep voter frustration with the economy, particularly the high cost of food, gasoline and housing.

Inflation expectations in the year ahead improved but remained elevated. Consumers expect prices to rise 4.3% over the next year, a three-month low. They also saw costs climbing at an annual rate of 3.4% over the next five to 10 years, also a step down from the prior month.

See also: US adds 165,000 jobs, topping all forecasts in broad advance

In addition to inflation worries, “consumers’ comments revealed growing anxiety over a possible AI bubble,” Joanne Hsu, director of the survey, said in a statement.

“The personal finances of consumers with the largest stock portfolios dropped 12% this month to their lowest reading since April, likely due to agitation in stock values in recent weeks, while all other wealth groups saw modest improvements,” she added.

A gauge of current personal finances climbed to a four-month high in November, while Americans' views of buying conditions for durable goods rebounded from a record low.

See also: Fed's Williams says should gather data to judge price risks

Gauges of current and expected conditions both rose to the highest since August.

The survey period includes responses from Oct 20 to Nov 2.

title: US tech stocks rebound as investors weigh valuations after rout
article:
(Nov 6): US stocks showed signs of stabilising Friday as dip buyers stepped in to support the battered artificial intelligence (AI) trade, though the severity of this week’s rout has left investors questioning whether the worst is over.

The Nasdaq 100 climbed 2.3% at 9.50am. in New York, pointing to an early rebound after the gauge posted its biggest one-day rout since the Covid pandemic. The S&P 500 rose 1%, while the Cboe VIX Index hovered near 24.14.

US job growth surged in October and the unemployment rate edged lower, a sign of labour-market strength in an expanding economy. Non-farm payrolls increased 165,000 last month, topping all forecasts, after an upward revision to the prior two months, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data out on Friday. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Stronger than expected labour report bolstered the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates next month.

Data show that systematic funds have been cutting their equity exposure and are now short US stocks. Commodity trading advisers, or CTAs, as well as other trend-following strategies likely deleveraged sharply and turned net short US equities, JPMorgan Chase & Co strategists led by Bram Kaplan said in a note.

“We had been telling people to hedge in the weeks leading up to this, and some of those clients are now removing the hedges as a way to get more exposure,” said Brian Nick, head of portfolio strategy at Newedge Wealth LLC. “For clients putting new money to work, we are continuing to emphasise quality.”

See also: Nasdaq 100 sinks 6% as chipmaker selloff deepens

In single-stock movers, Moderna Inc shares rose 2.5% after the vaccine maker boosted its revenue growth guidance for the full year. The firm also posted revenue for the third quarter that beat the average analyst estimate. Airbnb Inc jumped 9.8% after the online travel agency gave an outlook for fourth-quarter revenue that exceeded the consensus estimate. Lyft Inc shares dropped on Friday after the ride-hailing company gave a current quarter ride bookings and earnings forecast that came in largely in line with expectations.

Investors will probably keep ditching AI-related stocks even as the 15% selloff in semiconductor shares over the past two days likely prices in most of an anticipated decline in capital expenditures in the wake of Tuesday’s election results, according to Wells Fargo Securities strategist Ohsung Kwon.

See also: Nasdaq 100 sinks 5% as chipmaker sell-off deepens

The scale of this week’s reversal comes after a substantial wave of money flowed into equities. Bank of America strategists led by Michael Hartnett said US stock funds attracted US$92.3 billion in the four weeks through Wednesday, the biggest such inflow since June.

Hartnett and his team remain in a risk-off stance, saying they need to see central banks end interest-rate increases, the 10-year Treasury yield fall below 4.5% and oil prices drop under US$80 a barrel before turning more constructive on the outlook for financial conditions.

title: US Treasuries stumble as strong jobs data backs Fed-hike bets
article:
(Nov 6): Treasuries dipped after an unexpected surge in US job growth led traders to add to wagers that the Federal Reserve (Fed) will raise interest rates when officials next meet in December.

The declines on Friday pushed yields higher across maturities, with those on two-year notes — more sensitive to the outlook for the Fed’s rate path than longer peers — rising as much as seven basis points to 4.54%. The reaction faded quickly, however, leaving yields higher by one to six basis points, about where they were just before the data, which showed the US added 165,000 jobs in October, topping forecasts.

Traders maintained expectations for further rate increases by the US central bank, pricing in a roughly 80% chance of a quarter-point hike next month. All told, the market expects at least 40 basis points of additional tightening by September 2027.

The market’s relatively muted reaction to the data shows that “traders are wary of how equities will take this”, said John Briggs, head of US rates strategy at Natixis North America. “The market is clearly at the moment caught between risk-off flight-to-quality and an economy that continues to show resilience.”

Heading into the jobs report, Treasuries had erased a portion of this week’s steep gains that were driven by haven demand. The Democratic sweep of Congress in Tuesday’s US midterm elections escalated concerns around the sustainability of capital spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure, and investors flocked to bonds as shares of large technology companies slumped.

See also: Google debt-risk gauge rises as earnings revive AI debt jitters

A rotation from stocks to bonds that began a month ago intensified Thursday, sending the two-year yield below 4.5% and the 10-year towards 4.80%, the lowest levels since early September. Yields rebounded from those levels Friday before the jobs data as stock index futures pointed to gains for the cash market when it opens.

Non-farm payrolls rose 165,000 last month, beating a forecast gain of 65,000, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. Revisions for prior months were positive and wage growth also picked up to 3.1% for the past year.

The jobs “print leaves room for rates to back up if we shift back towards focusing on the fundamentals rather than seeing the move lower with the safe haven bid”, said Molly Brooks, US rates strategist at TD Securities. “If risk markets start to view strong data as bad news with expectations for higher rates, this could dampen some of the move higher in rates as flight to quality comes back into play.”

title: EU escalates TikTok probe over algorithmic ‘rabbit holes’
article:
(Nov 6): TikTok moved one step closer to a new European Union fine after regulators found its video-recommendation algorithm pushes users down “rabbit holes” of potentially harmful content, escalating an almost three-year probe into the video-sharing app.

TikTok users are repeatedly targeted with videos about topics they have previously engaged with, including on sensitive subjects like mental health struggles and body image, the European Commission said in preliminary findings on Friday. That can have a “detrimental impact” on users’ mental health, according to the statement from the EU’s executive branch.

The commission recommended ByteDance Ltd-owned TikTok alter the design of its central “For You” personalised feed. That includes taking users’ explicit preferences into account and potentially stopping using viewing time as a signal for recommending videos.

“Repeated exposure to such content may have serious negative effects on users’ well-being, including increased feelings of sadness or anxiety, body dissatisfaction, lower self-esteem, or worsening of existing eating disorders and mental conditions,” the commission said.

The case is part of a broader push by Brussels to curb features regulators say can make large-scale social media services addictive or expose children and vulnerable users to harmful material. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has separately unveiled plans to outlaw social media use for young teens.

“The Commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety,” TikTok said in a statement. “We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience.”

The findings escalate a wide-ranging investigation that began in February 2024 under the EU’s Digital Services Act, a sweeping rulebook requiring social networks and search engines to weed out illegal or harmful content.

The probe has increasingly zeroed in on the mechanics that has made the app so popular, with regulators focusing on TikTok’s infinite scroll, autoplay and the central “For You” personalised stream of videos.

Earlier this year, the commission concluded that TikTok’s design breached the DSA. These latest findings focus not on how TikTok keeps users scrolling, but what the algorithm shows them once it’s learned their interests.

See also: Grab to cut Vietnam driver fees, pay compensation after review

TikTok, owned by China’s ByteDance Ltd, failed to assess or mitigate the risks stemming from its recommendation system, according to the commission. The probe also scrutinises the platform’s handling of privacy and minor protections.

The preliminary findings mean that TikTok can respond to the commission and propose changes before regulators reach a final decision. If the commission concludes the platform broke the law, it can impose fines of as much as 6% of a company’s annual global sales.

The EU fined ByteDance €530 million (US$592 million or $758 million) in 2025 for illegally sending user data to China and €345 million in 2023 for lapses in the way it cares for children’s personal data.

title: US adds 165,000 jobs, topping all forecasts in broad advance
article:
(Nov 6): US job growth surged in October and the unemployment rate edged lower, a sign of labour-market strength in an expanding economy.

Non-farm payrolls increased 165,000 last month, topping all forecasts, after an upward revision to the prior two months, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data out on Friday. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%.

Employers across a broad range of sectors added jobs, including in professional and business services, healthcare and manufacturing. Overall private-sector payroll growth was the strongest since March.

Resilient consumer spending and strong business investment have supported demand and boosted corporate profits this year, encouraging companies to add more workers. Job growth has been uneven from month to month, but overall hiring has been strong enough to keep the unemployment rate low.

Federal Reserve officials will see one more jobs report and a full slate of inflation data before their next meeting in December. Investors expect them to raise interest rates at that gathering to counter inflation, following an increase in September and a subsequent decision to leave rates unchanged in October.

See also: Fed's Williams says should gather data to judge price risks

“This should allow the Fed to continue focusing on inflation and what’s happening in financial markets,” said Oscar Munoz, head of US economics at TD Securities. “To the extent that we see confirmation that we’re growing at 80,000 to 100,000 average job gains in the private sector, that would bode well not only for the labour market, but also for consumption.”

Fed chairman Kevin Warsh last week described employment conditions as “quite positive” and said the central bank was focused on prices. The yield on two-year Treasury notes rose and S&P 500 futures remained higher following the release.

Healthcare and social assistance employers added about 55,000 workers to payrolls in October, the most in six months. That sector has been the biggest driver of job growth in recent years.

See also: US voters reset debate on data centres and billionaires

Spending on data centres and demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related infrastructure has supported construction and manufacturing employment this year. Friday’s report showed that nonresidential construction firms continued to add jobs, even as broader construction payrolls were weighed down by losses in residential building.

Factory headcount also saw solid gains, with computer and electronic product manufacturing firms in particular adding the most jobs in four years.

Employment in the information and financial activities sectors, which have seen some of the fastest rates of job loss and AI adoption this year, showed tentative signs of stabilisation in October.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc economists, in a note published this week, said “AI’s labour market impact has become increasingly visible in recent months,” with “higher adoption associated with weaker job growth and higher unemployment” across nonmanufacturing industries.

“October hiring was strong and broad-based, and the upward revisions show the summer slowdown was milder than first reported. With unemployment edging down and wage growth firming, the labour market is not loosening the way we had anticipated. We still expect the Fed to hold in December on tighter financial conditions, but the risk of another hike has risen,” say Anna Wong, Andrew Sacher and Eliza Winger at Bloomberg Economics.

The report also suggested the labour market is generating little wage pressure. Average hourly earnings advanced 3.1% from a year earlier, matching the slowest pace since 2021. On a monthly basis, however, they rose 0.4%, topping forecasts.

The wage figures highlight a key source of voter frustration in this week’s midterm elections. While the unemployment rate has been low, pay hasn’t kept up with inflation throughout most of 2026.

The participation rate — the share of the population that is working or actively looking for work — edged up to 61.9% in October, the highest since March. A broad measure of unemployment also rose as the ranks of those working part-time for economic reasons jumped to a six-month high.

Measures of long-term unemployment worsened, with the median duration of a jobless spell reaching 11.9 weeks, the longest since 2021. Labour-market turnover has been historically low for much of the last few years, which has made it difficult to find new jobs and led many to feel either locked out or stuck in place.

The payroll numbers have seen wild swings this year from month to month, with sometimes large deviations from economists’ estimates. The median forecast in Bloomberg’s survey for the October report was off by 95,000, and four other reports this year have seen misses at least as large.

title: Bitcoin selloff eases as investors explore cautious recovery
article:
(Nov 6): Bitcoin edged back into the green after a bruising selloff on Thursday swept through cryptocurrencies and other risky assets, pressured by lacklustre chipmaker earnings and a Democratic sweep of Congress.

The largest cryptocurrency was trading at around US$76,000 on Friday morning in New York, having tumbled almost 6% from a position above US$80,000 a day earlier. Smaller cryptocurrencies were also broadly up on Friday, with BNB, ZCash and HYPE all trading up between 1% and 3%.

The S&P 500 recorded its steepest drop in more than a year on Thursday as investors forecast a Democrat-led clampdown on data centre expansion, pushing chipmaker stocks lower. Futures for the benchmark and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 crept up on Friday, helping to bolster trader optimism that spilled into crypto bets.

“Bitcoin appears to be finding some relief after yesterday’s [Thursday] sharp selloff, although I would be cautious about calling this a reversal just yet,” Dean Chen, an analyst at crypto exchange Bitunix, said in an email. “I would describe the current move as selling pressure easing, rather than fresh accumulation taking hold.”

Crypto remains on shaky ground after a US$6.3 billion hack on digital-asset exchange Binance Holdings Ltd rocked the sector on Oct 29, dampening investor enthusiasm for the asset class. Volatility in the broader market has only worsened the blow, with routs in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks spilling over to crypto as a result of many of the industry’s mining companies pivoting to the AI industry in recent years.

See also: Trump-linked crypto firm plans token buyback after midterm rout

“The selloff reflects growing doubts over the returns from huge AI spending, fears that tighter regulation could slow data-centre construction and a broader retreat from highly valued growth assets,” said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG. “Yet with stock markets continuing to slide, Bitcoin is so far holding its ground, suggesting buyers are stepping in to defend current levels. That relative strength could be an important test of whether Bitcoin is starting to decouple from the technology trade, rather than simply following it lower.”

Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds in the US recorded US$430 million in outflows on Thursday, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund led the pack with about US$200 million of that figure, followed by BlackRock Inc’s IBIT with about US$105 million in outflows.

“The selling does seem to be easing, but the recent bounce looks more like brief relief than sustained recovery,” said Samuel Leyne, co-head of crypto trading at Marex.

See also: Binance loses market share to crypto exchange rivals after hack

“You need a real catalyst to bring confidence back, whether that’s geopolitics cooling off, oil coming down or the macro picture improving,” he added. “Until then, we have to watch stocks, ETF flows and the basis levels. Bitcoin needs to get back above US$77,000 to build any momentum, and if equities keep sliding, US$75,000 is right back in play.”
